extracted.intended_audience: advertisers, advertising agencies, compliance officers, and legal counsel involved in U.S. advertising law and FTC enforcement
extracted.subtask_short: advertising compliance for U.S. FTC enforcement
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and enforcement standards used by the U.S. Federal Trade Commission to evaluate, substantiate, and remediate advertising practices, including definitions of deception and unfairness, substantiation requirements, and available remedies and liabilities. Intended to inform advertisers, agencies, and counsel about legal risk and compliance measures under the FTC Act and related rules (e.g., COPPA, endorsement guides).

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 5 authority (unfair or deceptive acts or practices)
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 5 of the FTC Act, 15 U.S.C. § 45 gives the Commission broad authority to prohibit 'unfair or deceptive acts or practices.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Forms the foundational statutory basis for FTC advertising enforcement; used to bring administrative and enforcement actions against deceptive or unfair advertising.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sections 12-15 restrictions on misleading claims for regulated products
rubrics_metrics.description: Sections 12-15 of the FTC Act, 15 U.S.C. §§ 52-55 prohibit the dissemination of misleading claims for food, drugs, devices, services or cosmetics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicable where advertising makes claims about foods, drugs, devices, services, or cosmetics; supports enforcement specific to these product categories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 13(b) injunction and equitable relief authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 13(b) of the FTC Act, 15 U.S.C. § 53 authorizes the Commission to file suit in United States District Court to enjoin an act or practice that is in violation of any provision of law enforced by the FTC.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enables district-court actions for injunctions, redress, disgorgement, and other equitable relief; often used to obtain preliminary injunctive relief and monetary remedies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of deception
rubrics_metrics.description: An advertisement is deceptive if it contains a misrepresentation or omission that is likely to mislead consumers acting reasonably under the circumstances to their detriment. Deceptive claims are actionable only if they are material to consumers’ decisions to buy or use the product, and the Commission need not prove actual injury to consumers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Materiality, reasonable consumer standard, and likelihood to mislead are key elements; case citations include Cliffdale Associates (Deception Policy Statement) and Kraft v. FTC.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of unfairness
rubrics_metrics.description: An advertisement or trade practice is unfair if it causes or is likely to cause substantial consumer injury which is not reasonably avoidable by consumers themselves and which is not outweighed by countervailing benefits to consumers or competition (15 U.S.C. § 45(n)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Commission may consider established public policies as evidence but such considerations may not serve as the primary basis for a determination; severity of injury, avoidability, and balance against benefits are the three-prong test.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cease-and-desist orders (administrative remedy)
rubrics_metrics.description: In advertising cases, the basic administrative remedy is a cease and desist order whose purpose is to enjoin the illegal conduct alleged in the complaint and to prevent future violations of the law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Voluntary cessation of an advertising campaign is not a defense to a Section 5 action (FTC v. Colgate-Palmolive); orders are crafted to stop present and deter future unlawful conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fencing-in remedies
rubrics_metrics.description: Fencing-in provisions allow the FTC to craft orders that 'close all roads to the prohibited goal,' e.g., restricting conduct beyond the specific product at issue to prevent circumvention of the order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts defer to Commission expertise unless remedy has no reasonable relation to unlawful practices; factors considered when fashioning fencing-in include seriousness of violation, violator's past record, and potential transferability of illegal practice to other products.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corrective advertising
rubrics_metrics.description: If merely prohibiting future misrepresentations will not dispel misperceptions conveyed through prior misrepresentations, the FTC may order corrective advertising to remedy consumer misperceptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used where prior deceptive claims created lasting misinformation; examples include orders requiring explicit corrective statements in future advertising and labels (e.g., Listerine case and representative corrective advertising cases).

rubrics_metrics.name: Informational remedies: disclosures, direct notification, and consumer education
rubrics_metrics.description: The FTC may require advertisers to make accurate information available through disclosures, direct notification (e.g., mailings to purchasers), or consumer education campaigns to correct or mitigate misinformation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Representative remedies include requiring warning labels, mailing notices to purchasers, distributing educational brochures, posting banner ads to inform consumers of rights, and targeted consumer education (examples and cases provided).

rubrics_metrics.name: Bans, bonds, and other structural remedies
rubrics_metrics.description: District courts have banned individuals from industries, required them to post bonds before engaging in business, or ordered other remedies (e.g., escrow accounts, monitors) to ensure future compliance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used for egregious or repeat offenders; examples include industry bans, escrow/performance bonds, suspended judgments with monetary penalties, appointment of monitors, and industry-specific prohibitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trade name excision
rubrics_metrics.description: The Commission has authority to forbid future use of a brand name or trade name when less restrictive remedies (like disclosures) would be insufficient to eliminate the deception conveyed by the name.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applied where a name itself is deceptive and cannot be cured by disclosure; case example ABS Tech Sciences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consumer redress and disgorgement (Section 13(b) and Section 19)
rubrics_metrics.description: District courts may order redress or disgorgement of profits under Section 13(b); the Commission may also seek redress under Section 19 if a Section 5 violation is found and the court finds the act 'dishonest or fraudulent.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Representative large monetary remedies and consent orders cited; used to compensate consumers and deprive violators of unjust gains.

rubrics_metrics.name: Civil penalties for violations of orders and trade regulation rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 5(l) authorizes the Commission to seek civil penalties for violations of cease and desist orders; Section 5(m)(1) authorizes civil penalties for violations of trade regulation rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts have imposed substantial civil penalties for order violations and trade rule breaches; representative cases show significant fines across sectors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enforcement through civil or criminal contempt
rubrics_metrics.description: Federal district court orders obtained by the FTC may be enforced through civil or criminal contempt, and the Commission has pursued criminal enforcement (Project Scofflaw) against violators of FTC-obtained orders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contempt enforcement can include fines and prison sentences for repeated or egregious violations of court orders; many representative cases cited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advertising Substantiation requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Advertisers must have a reasonable basis for making objective claims before dissemination; they must possess at least the level of substantiation expressly or impliedly claimed in the ad (Advertising Substantiation Policy Statement).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: First articulated in Pfizer and stated in Thompson Medical; applies across claim types with varying substantiation levels depending on claim seriousness and type.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pfizer factors for determining reasonable basis
rubrics_metrics.description: Six factors determine what constitutes a reasonable basis on a case-by-case basis: (1) the type of claim; (2) the benefits if the claim is true; (3) the consequences if the claim is false; (4) the ease and cost of developing substantiation for the claim; (5) the type of product; and (6) the level of substantiation experts in the field would agree is reasonable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to evaluate sufficiency of substantiation evidence when no specific level is claimed; heavier weight for claims with greater benefits or greater potential consumer harm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard of substantiation for health or safety claims
rubrics_metrics.description: For health or safety claims the Commission typically requires a relatively high level of substantiation, usually 'competent and reliable scientific evidence' defined as tests, analyses, research, studies, or other evidence based on expertise in the relevant area, conducted and evaluated objectively by qualified persons using generally accepted procedures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Surveys and placebo-effect studies are often insufficient; examples require adequate and well-controlled clinical testing or multiple well-controlled studies for certain drug claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advertiser (principal) liability standard
rubrics_metrics.description: An advertiser is responsible for all claims, express and implied, that are reasonably conveyed by the ad; the advertiser is strictly liable for violations of the FTC Act and proof of intent or actual consumer deception is not required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good faith reliance on advice of counsel is not a defense; advertisers must ensure all conveyed claims are substantiated and non-deceptive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Individual liability criteria for corporate officers
rubrics_metrics.description: Corporate officers may be held individually liable if they 'owned, dominated and managed' the company and if naming them individually is necessary to make the order fully effective; individuals are liable where they personally participated in or controlled the challenged acts or held a control position over employees who committed illegal acts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Knowledge can be actual knowledge, reckless indifference to falsity, or awareness of probability of fraud combined with intentional avoidance of truth; authority can be inferred from planning, decision making, supervision, or approving deceptive ads.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards for restitution/individual restitution liability
rubrics_metrics.description: Individuals are personally liable for restitution if they had knowledge that the corporation or an agent engaged in dishonest or fraudulent conduct, that misrepresentations were the type a reasonable person would rely on, and that consumer injury resulted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Knowledge may be shown by actual knowledge, recklessness, or deliberate ignorance; cases cited include Affordable Media and Publishing Clearing House.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advertising agency liability
rubrics_metrics.description: An advertising agency may be liable for a deceptive advertisement if it was an active participant in preparing the ad and if it knew or should have known that the advertisement was deceptive; agencies will be held to know what claims are conveyed to consumers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies need not independently re-test advertiser’s substantiation but cannot ignore obvious shortcomings or facial flaws in claims or substantiation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Liability for providing means and instrumentalities for deception
rubrics_metrics.description: Companies may be liable if they provide others with the means and instrumentalities for engaging in deceptive conduct (e.g., providing promotional materials, trade support that facilitates dissemination of deceptive claims).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Liability can attach to manufacturers, suppliers, or other upstream parties who enable deceptive marketing practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Liability of other parties (retailers, catalogers, infomercial producers, payment processors, home shopping)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Commission has held parties such as catalog marketers, retailers, infomercial producers, home shopping companies, and payment processors liable for their role in making or disseminating deceptive claims or engaging in deceptive trade practices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Liability arises where these parties materially participate in or disseminate deceptive claims or otherwise facilitate deceptive transactions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Endorsements and testimonials requirements (16 C.F.R. § 255)
rubrics_metrics.description: False or deceptive endorsements/testimonials violate Section 5; endorsements may not contain representations that would be deceptive or could not be substantiated if made directly by the advertiser. Endorsements are not themselves substantiation and any material connection between endorser and advertiser must be disclosed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advertisers must possess competent and reliable evidence to support efficacy representations conveyed via endorsements; material connections that might affect credibility must be disclosed to consumers.

rubrics_metrics.name: COPPA substantive requirements for websites directed to children
rubrics_metrics.description: Under COPPA (15 U.S.C. § 6501 et seq. and 15 C.F.R. § 312), websites must obtain verifiable parental consent before collecting, using, or disclosing personal information from children under 13; provide notice of information practices; give parents choice regarding disclosures; allow parental review and deletion; not require more information than is reasonably necessary; and maintain confidentiality, security, and integrity of kids’ data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Safe harbor programs approved by the FTC (e.g., CARU, TRUSTe, PRIVO) can provide a compliance pathway; representative COPPA enforcement cases demonstrate civil penalties for violations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Marketing to children: placement, targeting, and disclosure expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: FTC findings and reports expect industry to avoid placing ads for adult-rated/age-inappropriate products in media with substantial child/teen audiences, to provide rating information in advertising, and to limit target marketing to children; the industry should adopt codes that prohibit target marketing to children and impose sanctions for violations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow-up reports and mystery shopper surveys assess compliance; recommendations include expanding codes, limiting placements, increasing retail compliance, and enhancing parental understanding of ratings/labels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alcohol industry self-regulation recommendations
rubrics_metrics.description: FTC recommended that the alcohol industry create independent review boards to consider complaints, raise audience composition standards for ad placement (so adults are a larger percentage of audience), and adopt best practices to curb on-campus/spring break sponsorships, block underage website access, disallow placements on TV shows with large underage audiences, and restrict paid product placements to mature-rated movies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are recommended standards for voluntary industry self-regulation to reduce underage exposure to alcohol marketing.
